problem: The cause-and-effect sentence 'One processor cannot get much faster, so since the 1960s we buy more of them' muddles the timeline. Single-processor clock speeds kept rising for decades; parallel machines existed in the 1960s for other reasons, and buying many cores became the normal response only when single-core gains stalled in the 2000s.
fix: Rephrase, e.g.: 'Parallel machines have existed since the 1960s, but since single-core speeds stopped improving in the 2000s, buying more processors is the normal way to go faster.'

problem: Section 1 defines parallel computing as processors inside one machine that share one memory, but Section 2 lists 'a cluster' as a MIMD parallel machine and says 'the servers inside one rack are message passing'. A cluster is several machines with private memory, so the student sees the definition contradicted two paragraphs later.
fix: Add one clause in Section 1: 'Parallel machines are tightly coupled — usually one machine, usually shared memory. The same style of programming also runs on a cluster with message passing, which sits between the two columns of the table.'

problem: 'p = parallel time ÷ total serial time' is ambiguous, because 'serial' is used elsewhere in the chapter for the non-parallelisable fraction 1 − p. A student can read it as dividing by the serial part and get a nonsense value above 1.
fix: Write: 'p = time spent on the parallelisable part ÷ total time on one processor (the single-processor run).'

problem: The caption says the curves flatten at ceilings of 20×, 10× and 4×, but the y-axis stops at 16, so for p = 0.95 the curve only reaches about 15.4× at n = 64 and the 20× ceiling is never visible in the plot.
fix: Either raise the y-axis maximum to about 21 so the 20× ceiling is shown, or change the caption to say the p = 0.95 curve is still climbing towards its 20× ceiling at the right edge.
